title: Six Indian Cities Crack TasteAtlas Global Top 100, Mumbai Leads at Number Five
excerpt: Mumbai's street food culture propelled it into the top five of TasteAtlas's 2025-26 ranking of the world's best food cities, while Amritsar, New Delhi, Hyderabad, Kolkata, and Chennai also earned spots on the 100-city list.
body:
• Mumbai ranked fifth in TasteAtlas's 100 Best Food Cities 2025-26, the only Indian city in the global top 10.
  • Five more Indian cities — Amritsar (48th), New Delhi (53rd), Hyderabad (54th), Kolkata (73rd), and Chennai (93rd) — made the list.
  • Italian cities swept the top four spots, with Naples at number one, followed by Milan, Bologna, and Florence.
  • Indian street foods Parotta and Amritsari Kulcha also placed in the top 10 of TasteAtlas's global best street foods ranking.

Mumbai has claimed the fifth spot in TasteAtlas's 2025-26 ranking of the 100 best food cities in the world, making it the only Indian metropolis to break into the top 10. The ranking, compiled from millions of user reviews and expert evaluations across 17,073 cities and nearly 480,000 ratings of regional dishes, rewards cities with authentic, diverse, and culturally rooted food experiences.

Five other Indian cities joined Mumbai on the list: Amritsar at 48th, New Delhi at 53rd, Hyderabad at 54th, Kolkata at 73rd, and Chennai at 93rd. Together, they represent the broadest Indian presence the guide has recorded, spanning Mughlai, Punjabi, Hyderabadi, Bengali, and South Indian culinary traditions.

Mumbai's Street Food Culture Tips the Scale

TasteAtlas credited Mumbai's ranking primarily to its street food scene, calling it a vibrant melting pot of flavours drawn from Maharashtrian, Gujarati, Parsi, Goan, and South Indian communities. Vada pav, pav bhaji, bhelpuri, misal pav, and kheema pav were highlighted alongside festive specialities like modak.

Restaurants including Ram Ashraya, Shree Thaker Bhojanalay, Cafe Madras, and Baba Falooda were singled out as must-visit landmarks. Beyond the street stalls, TasteAtlas noted Mumbai's evolving fine-dining scene, food trucks, and café culture — from century-old eateries at Mohammed Ali Road to modern gastronomy-driven restaurants in Bandra and Lower Parel — as factors that strengthened its global standing.

"Mumbai's food culture is dynamic, inclusive, and deeply rooted in tradition."

— TasteAtlas, Best Food Cities 2025-26

From Amritsari Kulcha to Filter Coffee

Each of the other five Indian cities earned recognition for distinct culinary identities. Amritsar impressed with its ghee-laden kulchas, sarson ka saag, chole bhature, and lassi. Legendary eateries such as Kesar da Dhaba and Bharawan Da Dhaba continue to draw food tourists seeking authentic Punjabi meals.

New Delhi secured its spot on the strength of its Mughlai heritage and street-food scene. Butter chicken, kebabs, golgappa, and nihari anchored the city's reputation, with restaurants like Dum Pukht, Bukhara, and Saravana Bhavan representing its range.

Hyderabad, one spot behind Delhi at 54th, earned recognition for its Nizami culinary legacy, led by Hyderabadi biryani, haleem, and Chicken 65. Kolkata charmed global audiences with kathi rolls, rosogolla, mishti doi, and puchka, while Chennai rounded out India's presence with idli, dosa, filter coffee, and Chettinad cuisine.

Italian Dominance and the Global Picture

Italian cities dominated the top of the ranking. Naples took the number-one spot, followed by Milan, Bologna, and Florence — four of the top five cities worldwide were Italian. Paris ranked seventh, Vienna eighth, and Lima, Peru, rounded out the top 10.

In a separate TasteAtlas ranking of the world's best street foods, Indian dishes also stood out. Parotta placed fifth and Amritsari Kulcha sixth globally, ahead of street foods from dozens of countries. Chole Bhature ranked 40th.

What It Means for Indian Food Tourism

India's showing arrives at a time when food has become a primary driver of global travel decisions. According to TasteAtlas, tourists now plan restaurant visits before booking flights, and rankings like these shape destination choices for millions.

For the Indian diaspora, the recognition validates what many already know: that the flavours of home — from a ₹15 vada pav in Andheri to a slow-cooked haleem in the old city of Hyderabad — hold their own against any culinary tradition on the planet. Time Out's separate Best Cities for Food 2026 list reinforced the trend, placing Bengaluru at 13th worldwide for its diversity and dining confidence.

With six cities across five culinary traditions making the cut, India's food map is increasingly impossible for the global travel industry to ignore.
